source.title: Closed-Form Steepest Descent Direction toward Flat Minima: Reducing Upper Bounds on the Loss Hessian Eigenspectrum in Neural Networks
source.authors: Yuto Omae; K. Sakai; Yohei Kakimoto; Makoto Sasaki; Yusuke Sakai; Hirotaka Takahashi

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether controlling Hessian sharpness changes test performance, using a small binary-classification network and test macro F1; it does not test the specific interventions or measures in the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for HSR regularization, Hessian regularization, and A-SAM against plain gradient descent. Cited claims about other methods are not rows. Figure values are not stated numerically in the text.
record.test_reason: The study uses the flatness hypothesis to develop and evaluate HSR regularization, but tests none of V1–V8. Its closest connection is V7: it measures unscaled Hessian eigenvalues and test macro F1 in a small sigmoid network, rather than magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance and generalization-gap rankings among convolutional networks. Its method comparisons do not establish that version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate for the experiments. The authors' central contribution is a closed-form gradient of the WS upper bound. They report that HSR narrows the Hessian spectrum, avoids sharp minima and observed saddle-point behavior, and improves test macro F1 for Sharp Minima Seeds comparably to A-SAM, without reported adverse test effects for Flat Minima Seeds. The formulation is restricted to binary cross-entropy and a three-layer feedforward network.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a three-layer binary classifier, Gaussian synthetic data, and Hessian-spectrum regularization interventions; it does not test the cited claim versions' recipes or settings.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports different behavior for Sharp Minima Seeds versus Flat Minima Seeds; on the latter, methods have almost identical loss and eigenvalue behavior, and HSR is reported not to cause adverse effects.

fits_no_version.finding: For 113 selected Sharp Minima Seeds, all three regularization methods improve test macro F1 over plain gradient descent; A-SAM and HSR improve it more than Hessian regularization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sharpness-control interventions can improve held-out macro F1 in a small sigmoid binary classifier trained on 50 Gaussian examples.

fits_no_version.finding: For 113 selected Flat Minima Seeds, the authors report no adverse test-performance effect from HSR.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: HSR need not impair held-out performance for initializations already leading to flat minima in this synthetic setting.

fits_no_version.finding: All three regularization methods reduce the maximum Hessian eigenvalue for Sharp Minima Seeds; A-SAM and HSR are particularly effective.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hessian-spectrum control methods can reduce unscaled maximum Hessian eigenvalues in this small binary classifier.

record.problems: The experiment uses a small three-layer binary classifier, synthetic Gaussian data, 50 training examples, and 113 seeds per seed group. Figure-only values prevent extracting exact macro F1 scores and eigenvalue magnitudes; the text reports significance tests but not exact p-values.
record.rows_left_out: Training dynamics and decision-boundary results in Figs. 10, 11, and 15 are not separately extracted because the text does not state numerical outcomes for each method and condition beyond the summarized comparisons recorded above. Other eigenspectrum statistics in Figs. 12B–D are not separately rowed because they do not measure a claim version and are not needed for the extracted generalization results.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label held-out accuracy, and chance-level random-label generalization under matched recipes.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers, local connectivity, and convolution-derived initialization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning and optimizer-recovery interventions.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe changes that remove the penalty.
Dropout effects, training-set-size dependence, excessive dropout, and dropout/weight-decay removal with augmentation.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, training–test error gaps among comparably fitted convolutional networks, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples. The discussion of omitting confidently predicted examples from gradient computation does not test this.

record.verdict_notes: All rows remain unlinked. Their cannot_determine states concern the listed claim versions, not a denial of the qualitative method effects explicitly reported in the text. The seed groups were selected from the extremes of baseline sharpness among deduplicated converged critical points; they are not an unselected sample of initializations. Exact figure values and significance comparisons cannot be recovered from the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers compared with SGD under different tuning regimes.
Large-batch training and changes to the training recipe.
Magnitude-aware weight perturbations and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test accuracy.
